# Simulation framework {#sec-sim-framework}

This thesis uses an acceptance loop which has been further developed from the loop
described in @kozdoi_et_al_BE_BASL. Here I try to make very transparent how I modeled
each component, so that the reader may judge whether my assumptions and formulation from
the previous section are reflected in the simulations.

## Applicants' population {#sec-app-population-simulation}

Recalling section @sec-measure-theoretic-desc-ri-problem, according to
the probabilistic model for the RL problem it suffices to define the
distributions of the repayment outcome and the features to define the applicants'
population. In the simulation I do not consider latent features (case $f_l = 0$).
Further let $\tilde{Y} := Y | \{\epsilon = \text{no external effect}\}$ denote
the "noiseless" repayment outcome. I describe the population with this variable,
since it is less convoluted, is the object that the scorecard will
attempt to model and is easily bridged to the idea of a good and bad applicants.
The clean model corresponds to the classical two class multivariate Gaussian problem
of linear discriminant analysis (LDA). It might feel out of the decade to use such a simple
DGP, however using the very well known statistical properties of this model allows
carefully study the RI-problem very carefully.

It holds 
$$
\tilde{Y} \sim Bernoulli(\pi_{b})
$$ {#eq-Y-tilde-unconditional}
with $\pi_b \in (0,1)$
the probability of a bad applicant. The observable features vector $X$^[
    Recall from @eq-X-joint-observable-feats-vec: $X = \left(X_m^{\top}, X_h^{\top} \right)^{\top}$
]
is defined as a Gaussian Mixture with two components, a good one (paying population)
and a bad one (defaulters). With $o \in \{g, b\}$ we can characterize the distributions
of these populations as
$$
X | \{\tilde{Y}=o\} \sim \mathcal{N}\left(
    \mu_o =
    \begin{pmatrix}
        \mu_{m, o} \\ \mu_{h, o}
    \end{pmatrix},
    \Sigma_o =
    \begin{pmatrix}
        \Sigma_{m, o} & \Sigma_{mh, o} \\
        \Sigma_{mh, o}^{\top} & \Sigma_{h, o}
    \end{pmatrix}
\right)
$$
with $\Sigma_o, \Sigma_{m, o}$ and $\Sigma_{h, o}$ strictly positive definite (so, non-singular).
Letting $X_o$ be short for $X | \{\tilde{Y}=o\}$ also let $\phi_{X_o}$ denote its probability density
function (pdf). Since $X_o$ is normally distributed the pdf is given by
$$
\phi_{X_o}(x) := 
\frac{1}{\sqrt{(2\pi)^f |\Sigma_o|} }
\exp\left\{-\frac{1}{2} (x-\mu_o)^\top \Sigma_o^{-1} (x-\mu_o)\right\}
$$

For further analysis it is also helpful to write down the characterization of the joint distribution
of $(X,\tilde{Y})$, which is the marginal distribution of $\mathbb{P}_{X_m, X_h, X_l, Y}$ over the latent
feature component, given $\epsilon = \text{no external effect}$. Its density^[
    Following @Pollard_2001 [Ch. 3, Sec. 1], densities are understood here in the Radon–Nikodym sense,
    such that absolute continuity with respect to Lebesgue measure alone is not required, but can be
    given with respect to any dominating measure.
] is defined as a Radon-Nikodym derivative, using that the normal distribution is absolutely continuous
w. r. t. the Lebesgue Measure, in this case $\lambda^f$ over $\mathbb{R}^f$, and the discreteness of $Y$
$$
p_{X, \tilde{Y}} = \frac{d\mathbb{P}_{X, \tilde{Y}}}{d\left(\lambda^f \otimes \#_Y\right)}
$$
where $\#_Y$ is the counting measure over $E_Y$, which gets evaluated pointwise as a map
$\mathbb{R}^f \times E_y \to [0, \infty)$
$$
p_{X, \tilde{Y}}(x, o) = \pi_o \cdot \phi_{X_o}(x)
$$ {#eq-join-density-x-tilde-y}
where $\pi_g := 1 - \pi_b$.

From this we can easily derive the marginals^[
    Since $\pi_b \in (0, 1)$ and $\phi_{X_o}$ is strictly positive *and*
    finite everywhere, the marginal densities of $\mathbb{P}_{X, \tilde{Y}}$ over
    $X$ and $\tilde{Y}$ each are well-defined [@Pollard_2001, Ch. 4, Theorem 12]
] as
$$
p_{\tilde{Y}}(o) = \int_{\mathbb{R}^{f}} p_{X, \tilde{Y}}(x, o) \, \lambda^f(dx) = \pi_o ,
$${#eq-marginal-of-Y}
which of course corresponds to the probability mass function of a Bernoulli
distributed variable, and
$$
p_X(x) = \int_{E_Y} p_{X, \tilde{Y}}(x, y) \, \#_{Y}(dy) = \pi_b \phi_{X_b}(x) + \pi_g \phi_{X_g}(x)
$${#eq-marginal-of-X}

which is the pdf of a Gaussian Mixture and thus finally:
$$
\mathbb{P}(\tilde{Y} = o | X=x) = p_{\tilde{Y} | X} (o, x) = \frac{\phi_{X_o}(x) p_{\tilde{Y}}(o)}{p_X(x)}.
$${#eq-posterior-of-Y}

As known from LDA, we can quickly see from @eq-posterior-of-Y that a LR estimating
$\mathbb{P}(\tilde{Y} = b | X=x)$ having access to all covariates, has a functional
form that with proper parameter choosing would deliver exactly @eq-posterior-of-Y.^[
    See @hastie2009elements Ch. 4 for more details
]
Considering the consistency of LR under regularity conditions
and that LR is widely used in real life credit scoring applications, it evidences a further
reason to choose this DGP: we can expect LR to be very good approximator of the posterior.

Now let us assume that $\epsilon, \varepsilon$ are Bernoulli distributed
with parameters $\pi_{\epsilon} := \mathbb{P}(\epsilon =\text{no idiosyncratic shock}) > 0$
and $\pi_{\varepsilon, b} := \mathbb{P}(\varepsilon = b) \in (0,1)$. 
With this we can further write down
$$
\mathbb{P}(Y = b | X = x) = p_{Y=b | X}(x) = 
    \pi_{\epsilon} \, p_{\tilde{Y} | X} (b, x) +
    (1 - \pi_{\epsilon}) \pi_{\varepsilon, b}
$${#eq-pd-with-shock-perf-bayes}
which is the basis for the best possible prediction of a bad loan.

However, since the FI ignores $X_m$ for the scorecard creation, $s_t$ in reality can
only approximate $\mathbb{P}(Y = b | X_m = x_m)$. This distribution can also get quickly
calculated similarly by integrating out $X_h$ from the steps above, see for example
that we can write $x = \left(x_m^\top, x_h^\top \right)^\top$ in @eq-join-density-x-tilde-y, such that
$$
p_{X_m, \tilde{Y}} (x_m, o) :=  \int_{\mathbb{R}^{f_h}} p_{X, \tilde{Y}}(x, o) \lambda^{f_h}(d x_h)
$$

from that it follows that
$$
X_{m,o} := X_m | \tilde{Y} = o \sim \mathcal{N} \left(\mu_{m, o}, \Sigma_{m, o} \right)
$$ {#eq-marginal-of-X-m}
which is just the RV induced by a marginal distribution of $X$. Then we can calculate
that
$$
\mathbb{P}(Y = b | X_m = x_m) = p_{Y=b | X_m}(x_m) = 
    \pi_{\epsilon} \,
    \underbrace{\frac{\phi_{X_{m, b}}(x_m) p_{\tilde{Y}}(b)}{p_{X_m}(x_m)}}_{
        =: p_{\tilde{Y} | X_m} (b, x_m)
    }
    +
    (1 - \pi_{\epsilon}) \pi_{\varepsilon, b}
$${#eq-pd-with-shock-perf-bayes-reduced-model}

which does represent the best estimation we can hope to get from $s_t$.

For the simulation I have chosen a fairly simple DGP, so that its
statistical properties are easily understood. Namely, $f_m = 2$, $f_h = 1$,
$\Sigma_g = \Sigma_b = \Sigma$, such that the distributional differences
between $X_o$ and $X_g$ are solely characterized by the mean difference. I also
set $\pi_{\epsilon} = 1$, meaning no idyiosincratic shocks are considered.^[
    Although this decision seems arbitrary and maybe even oversimplifying consider that
    this case would deliver the same decision boundary under symmetric idiosnycratic shocks
    , i.e. $\pi_{\varepsilon, b} = 0.5$, which is arguably the most natural way to model the shocks.
    Therefore in this case having a $\pi_{\epsilon} < 1$ would only generate a higher variance
    of $Y \mid X$ (see that a bernoulli variable has its highest variance when the parameter is
    exactly $0.5$), which would make the classification problem more difficult but it would
    be less interesting and almost irrelevant when studying the RI problem from a dynamic
    perspective. Specially considering that LR is robust to class outliers
    [@hastie2009elements, Ch. 4]
]
The covariance matrix is characterized as follows
$$
\Sigma(\sigma_{m, 12}, \sigma_{mh}) = 
\Sigma = \begin{pmatrix}
1 & \sigma_{m, 12} & \sigma_{mh} \\
\sigma_{m, 12} & 1 & \sigma_{mh} \\
\sigma_{mh} & \sigma_{mh} & 1
\end{pmatrix}
$$ {#eq-general-form-Sigma}

and the means are given by
```{python}
#| notebook-links: false
tex_obj_g, _ = dgp_base.good_mixture.univariate_mixture_as_tex("g")
mu_g = tex_obj_g[tex_obj_g.find("\\mu"):tex_obj_g.find(", \\Sigma")]

tex_obj_b, _ = dgp_base.bad_mixture.univariate_mixture_as_tex("b")
mu_b = tex_obj_b[tex_obj_b.find("\\mu"):tex_obj_b.find(", \\Sigma")]

mus_report_str = (
    "$$\n" + mu_b + ", \\; " + mu_g + ".\n$$"
    + " {#eq-mus-chosen}"
)

display(Markdown(mus_report_str))

bayes_err_full_base = dgp_base.bayes_error_under_equal_covs().item()
bayes_err_str = f"{bayes_err_full_base*100:.2f}"

sigma_m12 = dgp_base.bad_mixture.cov[0,1].item()
sigma_m12_str = f"{sigma_m12:.1f}"
wished_corr_str = f"{wished_corr:.1f}"

min_corr_str = f"{all_corrs.amin().item():.1f}"
max_corr_str = f"{all_corrs.amax().item():.1f}"
```

The form in @eq-general-form-Sigma for the variance covariance matrix was selected
since it allows to study the full space of positive definite variance covariance
matrices in this form in order to choose sensible values for $\sigma_{m, 12}$ and
$\sigma_{mh}$. A useful way is to look at the performance of the classifiers given
by @eq-pd-with-shock-perf-bayes and @eq-pd-with-shock-perf-bayes-reduced-model, which
are the bayes classifiers^[
    Also known as "the generative model" in the LDA-literature.
]
for $Y | X$ and $Y | X_m$ respectively. Their (theoretical) performance can be
measured as their (Bayes) error rate, which is the probability that the classifier
makes a wrong classification, given that the decision rule is to predict bad if
the predicted probability of bad is higher than the predicted probability of good and
otherwise predicts good.^[
    See that this rules does not allow for the option "do not predict anything"
]
This probability can be analyitically calculated with @eq-bayes-error-rate-formula
as derived in the appendix (see @sec-derivation-bayes-rate). Let $P_e^{*}$ denote
the error rate of the full model - so following @eq-pd-with-shock-perf-bayes- and
$P^m_e$ the error rate of the reduced model according to @eq-pd-with-shock-perf-bayes-reduced-model.

In general it holds $0 \leq P_e^{*} \leq P^m_e$ and because of the properties of
Gaussian distributions, $P^m_e$ does not depend on $\sigma_h$. Using this properties
we can check the distribution of these error rates for all admissible $\Sigma$ matrices,
namely all positive definite ones. This set can also be analitically calculated using
@eq-positive-definite-region (see @sec-set-pos-definite-vcovs in the appendix for the
derivation). In @fig-all-bayes-errs the results of this analysis is shown.

```{python}
#| label: fig-all-bayes-errs
#| fig-cap: "Representation of joint distribution $(Y, X)$"
from thesis.helper_scripts.sensitivity_analysis import wrapper_bayes_errors_plot
wrapper_bayes_errors_plot(
    max_corrs=500,
    var_to_hide=base_sim["var_to_hide"],
    vcov=dgp_base.bad_mixture.cov,
    simulated_corrs=base_sim["corr_to_hidden"],
    idx_wished_corr=idx_wished_corr
)
```

In the left panel we see the heat map of the ratio $P_e^{*}/P^m_e$. The graphic shows
numerically that
$$
\forall \sigma_{m, 12} \exists \sigma_{mh} : P_e^{*}=P^m_e
$${#eq-equal-error-rates}

and for many of the cases it does not require the error rate to be zero. As it will be explained
in @sec-the-acceptance-loop
, the MNAR-ness will be modeled via overwrites in dependence of
extreme values of $X_h$. This kind of mechanism naturally induces a missing variable bias,
but the cases in @eq-equal-error-rates allow to study a classification case where the hidden
variable bias should be negligible in the following sense. A DGP with $P_e^{*}=P^m_e$
implies that for this DGP there exists a classifier depending solely on $X_m$ that
has a discriminatory power as good as a classifier using the full features vector.
Further, see that the joint distribution $(Y, X_m)$ as a marginal of $(Y, X)$ is in itself
also a LDA-type of DGP,^[
    This is evident from @eq-marginal-of-X-m together with the fact that the unconditional
    distribution of $Y$ does not get changed by integrating out $X_h$
] which can be consistently estimated by a technique like LR.

With these observations it became clear that it was sensible to choose a $\sigma_{m, 12}$
for which @eq-equal-error-rates would be fulfilled without the error rates being zero.
In order to do a good analysis of the MNAR effect in relationship with the inevitable
missing variable bias, it was sensible to choose a $\sigma_{m, 12}$ with a wide range of
values of $P_e^{*}/P^m_e$ for a granular control of the effect of the omitted variable and
with a relatively high $P^m_e$, so that the ratio differences also imply important differences
in the achievable Bayes rate and the classification problem does not become too trivial.
As depicted in the middle panel it was set $\sigma_{m, 12} = `{python} sigma_m12_str`$.

The final step is choosing $\sigma_{mh}$, which was done analyzing the right panel. For the
"base simulation", meaning the base case from which every sensitivity analysis will follow,
a value with resulting negligible omitted variable bias was selected, namely
$\sigma_{mh} = `{python} wished_corr_str`$. For the base simulation is then


Other values to be used later in the analysis
were selected as a grid with equidistant points from `{python} min_corr_str` to
`{python} max_corr_str`. For the base simulation is then 
$P_e^{*}=P^m_e= `{python} bayes_err_str`\%$.



We can see a visualization of the complete base dgp in @fig-3d-base-dgp, whereby the
Perfect Bayes Boundary corresponds to the classification boundary of a classifier given by 
@eq-pd-with-shock-perf-bayes. This boundary is calculated in the appendix
(see @sec-dec-boundary-perf-bayes-idyiosincratic-shocks) and can be rewritten from @eq-decision-boundary-equal-covs as the hyperplane $\mathcal{D}^*$ defined by
$$
W x - \beta = \log c
$${#eq-hyperplane-decision-boundary}
with $W=(\mu_b - \mu_g)^\top \Sigma^{-1} = \Sigma^{-1}(\mu_b - \mu_g)$,
$\beta = W\frac{\mu_b + \mu_g}{2}$ and $c$ a real constant depending on
the idyiosincratic schock dynamics ($\pi_{\epsilon}$ and $\pi_{\varepsilon, b}$)
and the unconditional probability of default ($\pi_b$).

```{python}
#| label: fig-3d-base-dgp
#| fig-cap: "Representation of joint distribution $(Y, X)$"
from thesis.helper_scripts.dgp_plotting import (
    extract_dgp_info_for_boundaries,
    plot3d_with_perf_bayes_boundary
)
dgp_info_for_boundaries = extract_dgp_info_for_boundaries(dgp_base)
plot3d_with_perf_bayes_boundary(dgp_base, dgp_info_for_boundaries["W"], dgp_info_for_boundaries["bias"])
```

Considering the bayes error rate of the problem, the good separability by the
hyperplane of the perfect bayes decision boundary observable in @fig-3d-base-dgp,
even more evidence can be given to argue that a LR should not have any problem calculating
the separation boundary, given all relevant variables. To check
out how difficult the problem gets while ignoring one of the variables, a pairwise
component plot as in @fig-pairwise-base-dgp is a good diagnostic. There, two decision
boundaries are plotted. The first one is a projection of $\mathcal{D}^*$ into a two
dimensional plane by setting the component not in the pairwise plot to its expected value.
Meaning with $r$ component's position in $X$ of the
non-shown component, it was set in @eq-hyperplane-decision-boundary
$$
x\mathtt{[r]} = \mathbb{E}(X | \epsilon = \text{no shock})\mathtt{[r]} = (\pi_b)\mu_b\mathtt{[r]} + (1-\pi_b)\mu_g\mathtt{[r]}.
$$
The other boundary is called $\mathcal{D}^r$ and corresponds to the decision boundary if
the non-shown component was integrated out of the joint distribution and then given such a
DGP calculating the boundary of the byes classifier.

Through @fig-pairwise-base-dgp we can see in the left panel that the projected $\mathcal{D}^*$
and $\mathcal{D}^r$ return the same decision boundary when considering only $X_m$. Furhter,
the projections of $\mathcal{D}^*$ in the middle and right panels show a line (almost)
parallel to the $X_h$ axis in both cases, which shows that the bayes classifier with full
information ignores that variable. However in both of those panels the $\mathcal{D}^r$
differ from the projected one, showing that although the full information model ignores
$X_h$, it still contains relevant information on the repayment outcome. This conclussion
can of course also be obtained from eyeballing the data structure in those panels. All of
these observations strengthen the argument for using this DGP with overwrites based on
$X_h$ as a way to generate an MNAR-mechanism without inducing any (relevant) omitted variable
bias.

It is clear that @fig-pairwise-base-dgp also suggests that the classification
problem shoud also be well solved by a logistic regression considering only two
of the components of $X$. This figure also shows a bit the importance of $X_h$ 
for the classification problem in relationship to the correlation to $X_{m}$.
See that the classification boundary in the graphs containing $X_h$ has a positive
slope w. r. t. $X_{m,1}$ and $X_{m, 2}$. This means that a higher (positive)
correlation of the hidden factor to the model variables increases the separation
power when observing $X_h$. A negative correlation should approximately have the
opposite effect.

```{python}
#| label: fig-pairwise-base-dgp
#| fig-cap: "Pairwise covariates component representation of $Y, X$"
from thesis.helper_scripts.dgp_plotting import plot_pairwise_dgp_with_perf_bayes_boundaries
plot_pairwise_dgp_with_perf_bayes_boundaries(dgp_base, **dgp_info_for_boundaries)
```

As a final remark, I believe it is important to make transparent how the sampling of
$\mathbb{P}_{X,Y}$ is done, as this study is mostly numerical and therefore the simulation
implementation should also be looked critically upon. The used logic is summarised in algorithm
\ref{alg:sampling-x-y}.
First the realizations of $Y$ are sampled from a Bernoulli distribution as defined in
@eq-Y-tilde-unconditional. These values are effectively reorganized to be able to have
contiguous memory buffers later for the features' realizations, increasing its efficiency.
Then the corresponding amount of samples from $X_{b}$ and $X_g$ are sampled^[
    For MVN sampling the standard methodology via cholesky decomposition of $\Sigma$ and
    standard white noise was used. See for example @wiki:multivariate_normal_sampling
    for another wording of this method.
] 
and stacked together, which allows to cheaply mantain the order. At the end the 
realizations are returned.

\begin{algorithm} 
\caption{Sampling from $\mathbb{P}_{X, Y}$}
\label{alg:sampling-x-y}
\begin{algorithmic}[1]
    \Statex \textbf{Note:} Here the random variables and their realizations are represented with the same notation for convenience
    \Procedure{CreditDGP.sample}{$\sigma_{m,12}, \sigma_{mh}, \pi_b, n$}
        \Statex \textbf{1. Sampling good and bad components} while ensuring contiguous memory per class
        \State $\forall i \in \{1, \ldots, n\}: B_i \overset{iid}{\sim} \operatorname{Bernoulli}(\pi_b) \in \{0, 1\}$ with $\mathbb{P}(B_i = 1) = \pi_b$
        \State $n_b \gets \sum_{i=1}^n B_i$, $n_g \gets n - n_b$
        \State $\mathbf{Y} \gets (\underbrace{b, \ldots, b}_{n_b \text{ times}}, \underbrace{g, \ldots, g}_{n_g \text{ times}})$
        \Comment{$\mathbf{Y} \in \{b, g\}^{n}$}
        
        \Statex \textbf{2. Multivariate Gaussian sampling} for goods and bads
        \State $\Sigma_{chol} \gets \operatorname{CholeskyDecomposition(\Sigma(\sigma_{m,12}, \sigma_{mh}))}$ \Comment{See \eqref{eq-general-form-Sigma}}
        
        \For{$o \in \{b, g\}$}
            \State $\mathbf{m}_o \gets ( \mu_o, \ldots, \mu_o)^\top \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times f}$
            \State $\mathbf{E} \gets (E_1, \ldots, E_n)^\top$, $\forall j \in \{1, \ldots, n\}: E_j \overset{iid}{\sim} \mathcal{N}(0_f, I_f)$
            \Statex \Comment{Done via i.i.d. sampling of $n\cdot f$ univariate standard normals}
            \State $\mathbf{X}_o \gets \mathbf{m}_o + \mathbf{E} \Sigma_{chol}^\top$
        \EndFor

        \State $\mathbf{X} \gets \begin{pmatrix}\mathbf{X}_b \\ \mathbf{X}_g\end{pmatrix}$
        \State \Return $\mathbf{X},\, \mathbf{Y}$ 
    \EndProcedure
\end{algorithmic} 
\end{algorithm}

## The acceptance loop {#sec-the-acceptance-loop}

To visualize exactly how the acceptance loop was created it is helpful to look directly
to the complete loop, after defining the applicant's distribution. In Algorithm
\ref{alg:ac-forward-pass}
the whole process can be seen. 

\begin{algorithm} 
\caption{Actor-Critic Forward Pass}
\label{alg:ac-forward-pass}
\begin{algorithmic}[1] 
    
    \Procedure{ActorCritic}{$A_{t-1}, M_{t-1}$}
        \State $\mathbf{P} \gets [\ ]$, $A_t \gets [\ ]$ \Comment{$\mathbf{P}$roabilities and new $A$rchitecture lists}
        \State $H_t, M_t \gets \texttt{CriticLSTM}\left(A_{t-1}, \texttt{hx=}M_{t-1}\right)$
        \State $h_t \gets H_t\texttt{[-1, :]}$
        \State $\mathbb{P}_{N_{TSF}} \gets \operatorname{softmax}\left(\texttt{AH}_1^{MLP}\left(h_t\right)\right)$ \Comment{$\mathbb{P}_{N_{TSF}} \in \mathbb{R}^{\max \mathcal{N}_{TSF}}$}
        \State $N_{TSF} \gets \operatorname{MultiNomialSample}\left(\mathbb{P}_{N_{TSF}}\right)$
        \State $A_t\texttt{.append}\left(N_{TSF}\right)$
        \State $\mathbf{P}\texttt{.append}\left(\mathbb{P}_{N_{TSF}}\right)$
        \State $\text{LogProbSum} \gets \log\mathbb{P}_{N_{TSF}}\texttt{[}N_{TSF} \texttt{]}$
        \For{$\texttt{i}_A \in \{1, \ldots , N_{TSF}\}$}
            \State $\mathbb{P}_{\texttt{i}_A} \gets \operatorname{softmax}\left(W_t^{\texttt{i}_A, h}h_t + W_t^{\texttt{i}_A, p}\mathbf{P}\texttt{[-1]} + b_t^{\texttt{i}_A}\right)$ \Comment{$\mathbb{P}_{\texttt{i}_A} \in \mathbb{R}^{\#TSF}$}
            \State $TSF_{\texttt{i}_A} \gets 
            \operatorname{MultiNomialSample}\left(\mathbb{P}_{\texttt{i}_A}\right)$
            \State $\mathbf{P}\texttt{.append}\left(\mathbb{P}_{\texttt{i}_A}\right)$
            \State $A_t\texttt{.append}\left(TSF_{\texttt{i}_A}\right)$
            \State $\text{LogProbSum} \gets \text{LogProbSum} +  \log\mathbb{P}_{\texttt{i}_A}\texttt{[}TSF^e_{\texttt{i}_A} \texttt{]}$
        \EndFor
        \For{$\texttt{i}_A \in  \{1, \ldots , \max\mathcal{N}_{TSF}\} \setminus  \{1, \ldots , N_{TSF}\}$}
            \State $\operatorname{NoGrad}\left(W_t^{\texttt{i}_A, h}, W_t^{\texttt{i}_A, p}, b_t^{\texttt{i}_A}\right)$
        \EndFor
        \State $\mathbb{P}_{AG} \gets \operatorname{softmax}\left(W_t^{AG, h}h_t + W_t^{AG, p}\mathbb{P}_{N_{TSF}} + b_t^{AG}\right)$ \Comment{$\mathbb{P}_{AG} \in \mathbb{R}^{\#AG}$}
        \State $AG \gets \operatorname{MultiNomialSample}\left(\mathbb{P}_{AG}\right)$
        \State $\mathbf{P}\texttt{.append}\left(\mathbb{P}_{AG}\right)$
        \State $A_t\texttt{.append}\left(AG\right)$
        \State $\text{LogProbSum} \gets \text{LogProbSum} +  \log\mathbb{P}_{AG}\texttt{[}AG \texttt{]}$
        \State $V_{h_{t}} \gets \texttt{CriticPerceptron}\left(h_{t}\right)$ \Comment{Evaluate $h_{t}$ with Value Function}
        \State $\operatorname{SaveInClass}\left(\text{LogProbSum}, V_{h_{t}}\right)$
        \State \Return $\mathbf{P},\, A_t,\, M_t$ 
    \EndProcedure
\end{algorithmic} 
\end{algorithm}

## Acceptance loop algorithm
